lessons.title: Hallucination: Confident, Fluent, and Wrong
lessons.description: Understand why generative models produce false information with the same confidence as true information.

sections.title: What you should be able to do
sections.content: By the end of this lesson, you can explain why hallucination happens and why fluency is not evidence of correctness.

sections.title: 🎭 Fluency and correctness are separate properties
sections.content: A generative model is trained to produce plausible-sounding continuations, not to only ever state true facts — these are genuinely different objectives. **Hallucination** is when a model generates confident, fluent, but factually incorrect or fabricated content — a made-up citation, a wrong date, an invented API function that doesn't exist.

sections.title: 🧩 Why it happens (and why it's not easily 'fixed')
sections.content:
Recall the density-modeling framing from the start of this course: the model learned p(x), a distribution over plausible text, not a verified database of facts. When the model is uncertain, it doesn't know to say 'I don't know' by default — it produces the most statistically plausible-sounding continuation, which can be entirely fabricated while reading exactly as confidently as a correct answer.

```python
# There's no code fix for hallucination itself -- but retrieval-augmented
# generation (a dedicated later track) grounds answers in retrieved,
# verifiable source documents instead of relying purely on the model's
# internal, unverified knowledge
```

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.content:
**Trusting confident-sounding output as a proxy for correctness.** Confidence in tone is a property of fluent generation, not evidence of accuracy — these are unrelated.

**Assuming hallucination only happens on obscure topics.** It can happen on any topic, including ones where the model seems otherwise knowledgeable.

**Not verifying generated facts, citations, or code before relying on them.** Especially for anything high-stakes (legal, medical, financial, or production code), independent verification is not optional.

questions.question: What is 'hallucination' in the context of generative models?
options: A visual glitch that only occurs in image generation models
When a model generates confident, fluent, but factually incorrect or entirely fabricated content
A training technique used to improve model accuracy
An error that only occurs when temperature is set to exactly 0
questions.explanation: Hallucination refers to a model producing output that sounds fluent and confident but is factually wrong or made up — a real and well-documented limitation of generative language models.

questions.question: Why does a generative model's fluency give no guarantee that its content is accurate?
options: Fluency and accuracy are actually the same thing for a trained model
The model was trained to produce plausible-sounding continuations of text (density modeling), which is a different objective from verifying that stated facts are true
Fluent output is always automatically accurate by definition
Models cannot produce fluent output unless it's also accurate
questions.explanation: As covered in this course's density-modeling lesson, the model's objective is learning what plausible text looks like — not maintaining a verified store of facts — so fluency and factual correctness are genuinely separate properties that can diverge.

questions.question: Why is verifying generated facts, citations, or code independently especially important for high-stakes use cases?
options: Verification is never necessary because generative models are always accurate

Since a model can produce confidently wrong content indistinguishable in tone from correct content, independent verification is the only reliable way to catch a hallucination before it causes real harm
High-stakes use cases are actually immune to hallucination
Verification only matters for image generation, never for text
questions.explanation: Because a hallucinated fact reads with the exact same confident tone as a correct one, there's no way to distinguish them from the output alone — making independent verification essential wherever an error would carry real consequences (legal, medical, financial, production code).

questions.question: What is hallucination, as defined in this lesson?
options: When a model generates confident, fluent, but factually incorrect or fabricated content
A visual artifact that only occurs in diffusion-based image models
A training technique used to reduce a model's error rate
An error that only happens when temperature is set to 0
questions.explanation: The lesson defines hallucination as confident, fluent output that is factually incorrect or entirely made up, such as a fabricated citation or invented function.

questions.question: How does this lesson connect hallucination back to the density-modeling framing from earlier in the course?
options: The model learned p(x), a distribution over plausible text, not a verified database of facts
The model stores every training fact in a verified lookup table
Density modeling guarantees a model can never hallucinate
Hallucination only occurs in models that don't use density modeling
questions.explanation: The lesson explicitly recalls the density-modeling lesson: since the model learned a distribution over plausible text rather than a fact database, it can produce plausible-sounding but false content.

questions.question: What does the lesson suggest as a dedicated approach for grounding answers in verifiable sources, rather than relying purely on the model's internal knowledge?
options: Retrieval-augmented generation
Increasing the temperature parameter
Switching to greedy decoding
Disabling classifier-free guidance
questions.explanation: The lesson points to retrieval-augmented generation (a dedicated later track) as the approach for grounding answers in retrieved, verifiable source documents instead of unverified internal knowledge.

questions.question: Why is it a mistake to assume hallucination only happens on obscure topics, according to this lesson?
options: Because it can happen on any topic, including ones where the model otherwise seems knowledgeable
Because hallucination is physically impossible on well-known topics
Because only obscure topics have any associated training data at all
Because common topics are immune to fabricated content by design
questions.explanation: The lesson states plainly that hallucination isn't confined to obscure topics — it can occur even where the model otherwise appears to be knowledgeable.

questions.question: Why does this lesson stress that fluency in tone is not evidence of correctness?
options: Because confidence in tone is a property of fluent generation, not evidence of accuracy — these are unrelated
Because fluent output is always guaranteed to be factually correct
Because fluency and confidence are the same thing as accuracy
Because only unfluent output can ever be considered inaccurate
questions.explanation: The lesson's stated common mistake is trusting confident-sounding output as a proxy for correctness, when tone and factual accuracy are genuinely unrelated properties.

lessons.title: Bias Amplification in Generative Systems
lessons.description: See how training data biases can show up, and get amplified, in generated content.

sections.title: What you should be able to do
sections.content: By the end of this lesson, you can explain how bias enters a generative model and give an example of how it can show up in generated output.

sections.title: 📊 Models learn what's in the data, including its biases
sections.content: A generative model's p̂(x) approximates whatever distribution its training data actually reflects — including historical, social, and representational biases present in that data. If certain demographics, viewpoints, or associations are over- or under-represented in training data, the model's generations tend to reflect (and can even amplify) those same patterns.

sections.title: 🔍 Amplification, not just reflection
sections.content: Bias in generative output isn't always a simple mirror of training data proportions — in some documented cases, models have been shown to *amplify* biases beyond what raw training data statistics would predict, associating certain roles, traits, or outcomes with specific demographic groups more strongly than the underlying data alone would suggest.

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.content:
**Assuming a technically accurate model is automatically a fair one.** Accuracy on a benchmark says nothing about whether generated content reflects unwanted bias.

**Treating bias as a one-time problem to 'fix' rather than an ongoing concern.** Bias evaluation needs to be part of continuous monitoring, not a single pre-launch checklist item.

**Assuming bias only affects text output.** Image generation models have documented bias issues too — for example, in how they depict people in different professions or roles.

questions.question: Why can a generative model's output reflect biases present in its training data?
options: Models are completely unaffected by any patterns in their training data
The model's learned distribution approximates whatever the training data actually contains, including historical, social, and representational biases present in that data
Bias only ever comes from the model's architecture, never from training data
Generative models are legally required to be unbiased regardless of training data
questions.explanation: Since a generative model learns p̂(x) from its training data, whatever biases exist in that data — over- or under-representation of certain groups or viewpoints — tend to be reflected in the patterns the model has learned.

questions.question: What does it mean for a model to 'amplify' bias rather than simply reflect it?
options: Amplification means the model perfectly mirrors training data proportions with no distortion
In documented cases, models have shown associations stronger than what raw training data statistics alone would predict, exaggerating certain patterns beyond the underlying data
Amplification only refers to increasing the volume of an audio generation model
Amplification is a technical term meaning the model has more parameters
questions.explanation: Amplification describes cases where a model's biased associations go beyond simply mirroring training data statistics — the learned patterns end up more skewed than the raw data proportions alone would suggest.

questions.question: Why is it a mistake to assume a technically accurate model is automatically a fair one?
options: Accuracy and fairness are actually the same measurable property
A model can perform well on accuracy benchmarks while still producing biased content, since accuracy and bias evaluate fundamentally different aspects of a model's behavior
Fairness is not a real concern for any trained model
Bias only matters for classification models, not generative ones
questions.explanation: Accuracy measures how well a model performs its stated task, which is an entirely separate question from whether its generated content reflects unwanted bias — a model can score well on one while still failing badly on the other.

questions.question: Why can a generative model's output reflect biases present in its training data, according to this lesson?
options: Because the model's learned distribution approximates whatever the training data actually contains, biases included
Because bias only ever comes from the model's architecture, never its data
Because generative models are legally required to remove all bias automatically
Because models are completely unaffected by patterns in their training data
questions.explanation: The lesson explains that since a model's p̂(x) approximates its training data's distribution, any historical, social, or representational biases in that data tend to be reflected in the model's outputs.

questions.question: What does it mean for a model to 'amplify' bias, as opposed to simply reflecting it, per this lesson?
options: In documented cases, models have shown associations stronger than what raw training data statistics alone would predict
Amplification means the model perfectly mirrors training data proportions with zero distortion
Amplification refers exclusively to increasing an audio model's output volume
Amplification means a model completely removes all bias from its output
questions.explanation: The lesson describes amplification as models showing associations skewed beyond what the raw training data proportions alone would suggest, not just a simple reflection of those proportions.

questions.question: Why is it a mistake to assume a technically accurate model is automatically a fair one, according to this lesson?
options: Because a model can perform well on accuracy benchmarks while still producing biased content — these are separate aspects of behavior
Because accuracy and fairness are mathematically identical measurements
Because fairness is not a real concern for any trained model
Because bias only ever affects classification models, never generative ones
questions.explanation: The lesson explains that accuracy measures task performance, which is entirely separate from whether generated content reflects unwanted bias — a model can score well on one while failing badly on the other.

questions.question: Why does the lesson say bias evaluation should be an ongoing concern rather than a one-time fix?
options: Because treating bias as a single pre-launch checklist item misses how it needs continuous monitoring over time
Because bias, once measured, never needs to be checked again
Because bias evaluation is only relevant during model training, never after deployment
Because ongoing monitoring has no effect on catching biased behavior
questions.explanation: The lesson warns against treating bias as a one-time problem to fix, recommending continuous monitoring rather than a single pre-launch checklist item.

questions.question: Why does the lesson caution against assuming bias only affects text output?
options: Because image generation models have documented bias issues too, such as in how they depict people in different professions
Because image models are entirely immune to any form of bias
Because bias can only ever manifest in generated audio
Because text is the only modality where training data has any influence
questions.explanation: The lesson explicitly notes that image generation models have their own documented bias issues, such as skewed depictions of people in certain professions or roles.

lessons.title: Deepfakes and Misuse Risks
lessons.description: Understand the specific misuse risks that come with realistic synthetic media.

sections.title: What you should be able to do
sections.content: By the end of this lesson, you can describe what a deepfake is and name a couple of mitigation approaches being developed.

sections.title: 🎭 Realistic synthetic media, used to deceive
sections.content: A **deepfake** is synthetic media (image, audio, or video) generated to convincingly depict a real person doing or saying something they didn't actually do or say. The same generative techniques covered in this course (diffusion for images/video, TTS-style generation for audio, from the multimodal module) that enable legitimate creative and productivity uses also enable this specific, serious misuse.

sections.title: 🛡️ Mitigation approaches in development
sections.content: Approaches being developed and deployed to address this include: **provenance/watermarking** (embedding an invisible or visible signal marking content as AI-generated), **detection models** (trained specifically to spot synthetic media, an ongoing arms race against improving generators), and **platform policies** restricting the creation or distribution of non-consensual synthetic media of real people.

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.content:
**Assuming watermarking alone fully solves the problem.** Watermarks can potentially be stripped or may not survive certain edits, so no single technical mitigation is a complete solution on its own.

**Treating this as a purely theoretical, future risk.** Deepfake misuse (impersonation, fraud, non-consensual content) is a documented real-world problem today, not a hypothetical.

**Assuming detection will always keep pace with generation.** Detection and generation are in an ongoing arms race — a detector effective today isn't guaranteed to remain effective against newer generation techniques.

questions.question: What defines a deepfake?
options: Any image or video that was edited using traditional (non-AI) software
Synthetic media generated to convincingly depict a real person doing or saying something they didn't actually do or say
A specific file format used only for storing generated audio
A model architecture used exclusively for text generation
questions.explanation: A deepfake specifically involves generating realistic synthetic media that misrepresents a real, identifiable person — the deceptive depiction of a real individual is the defining, concerning feature.

questions.question: What is watermarking, as a proposed mitigation for synthetic media risks?
options: A technique that makes generative models incapable of producing realistic output
Embedding an invisible or visible signal into generated content that marks it as AI-generated
A method for training generative models faster
A legal requirement that eliminates all possible misuse automatically
questions.explanation: Watermarking embeds a signal (visible or invisible) into generated content to mark its synthetic origin, intended to help people and systems distinguish AI-generated media from authentic content.

questions.question: Why is it a mistake to assume detection models will always keep pace with generative models?
options: Detection models are always perfectly effective against every generation technique, forever
Detection and generation exist in an ongoing arms race, so a detector effective today is not guaranteed to remain effective as generation techniques continue to improve
Detection models are not actually used for this problem at all
Generation techniques stopped improving once detection models were introduced
questions.explanation: Since generative techniques continue to improve, detection approaches must also continually adapt — there's no guarantee that a detection method effective against current generators will remain effective against future ones, making this an ongoing arms race rather than a solved problem.

questions.question: What is the defining feature of a deepfake, according to this lesson?
options: Synthetic media generated to convincingly depict a real person doing or saying something they didn't actually do or say
Any video edited using traditional, non-AI software tools
A file format used exclusively for storing generated audio
A model architecture reserved only for text generation
questions.explanation: The lesson defines a deepfake specifically as synthetic media that deceptively depicts a real, identifiable person doing or saying something that didn't actually happen.

questions.question: What is watermarking, as a mitigation approach described in this lesson?
options: Embedding an invisible or visible signal into generated content that marks it as AI-generated
A technique that makes a generative model physically incapable of producing realistic output
A method exclusively for speeding up model training
A legal requirement that eliminates all possible misuse automatically
questions.explanation: The lesson describes watermarking as embedding a signal, visible or invisible, into generated content specifically to mark its synthetic, AI-generated origin.

questions.question: Why does this lesson describe detection and generation as being in an 'ongoing arms race'?
options: Because a detector effective today isn't guaranteed to remain effective as generation techniques continue to improve
Because detection models always permanently outperform every future generator
Because generation techniques stopped improving once detectors were introduced
Because detection and generation have no relationship to each other
questions.explanation: The lesson frames detection and generation as continually evolving against each other, meaning today's effective detector may not keep working against tomorrow's improved generators.

questions.question: Why does the lesson caution against treating deepfake misuse as a purely theoretical, future risk?
options: Because deepfake misuse, like impersonation and fraud, is a documented real-world problem today
Because deepfakes cannot technically be created with current technology
Because deepfake risk will only ever become relevant decades from now
Because misuse of synthetic media has never actually been observed
questions.explanation: The lesson explicitly states that deepfake-related misuse (impersonation, fraud, non-consensual content) is a real-world problem happening now, not a hypothetical future concern.

questions.question: Why is watermarking alone not described as a complete solution to synthetic media risks, per this lesson?
options: Because watermarks can potentially be stripped or may not survive certain edits
Because watermarking makes any misuse of synthetic media technically impossible
Because watermarking is the only mitigation approach that has ever been proposed
Because watermarks automatically detect and block all deepfakes
questions.explanation: The lesson warns against assuming watermarking alone fully solves the problem, since watermarks can be stripped or might not survive certain kinds of edits.

lessons.title: Evaluation and Red-Teaming Basics
lessons.description: Learn how teams proactively probe generative systems for failure modes before real users find them.

sections.title: What you should be able to do
sections.content: By the end of this lesson, you can explain what red-teaming is and why it complements, rather than replaces, standard evaluation metrics.

sections.title: 🎯 Standard evaluation checks the average case
sections.content: The metrics covered earlier in this course (perplexity, human evaluation, automated comparison metrics) mostly tell you how a system performs on typical, expected inputs. They don't tell you what happens when someone deliberately tries to break it.

sections.title: 🔴 Red-teaming: deliberately trying to break it
sections.content:
**Red-teaming** means having people (or automated systems) deliberately try to elicit bad behavior from a generative system — getting it to produce harmful content, leak sensitive information, generate convincing misinformation, or otherwise fail in ways standard evaluation wouldn't surface. This connects directly to the security-mindset thinking that appears again in the eval-and-security track later in the curriculum, applied here specifically to generative failure modes.

```python
# Conceptual red-team prompts probe for specific failure categories:
# - Can the system be tricked into ignoring its own safety instructions?
# - Does it leak information it shouldn't have access to?
# - Can it be steered into generating harmful or misleading content?
```

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.content:
**Treating red-teaming as a one-time pre-launch activity.** New failure modes get discovered continuously (including by real users after launch), so ongoing red-teaming matters, not just a single pre-release pass.

**Only testing for failure modes you already anticipated.** The most valuable red-teaming often surfaces failure modes the original team didn't think to look for.

**Confusing red-teaming with standard quality evaluation.** They're complementary: one asks 'how good is typical performance?', the other asks 'how badly can this be made to fail?'

questions.question: How does red-teaming differ from the standard evaluation metrics covered earlier in this course?
options: They are the exact same activity with a different name
Standard evaluation measures typical performance on expected inputs, while red-teaming deliberately tries to elicit bad or harmful behavior from the system
Red-teaming only applies to image generation, never to text
Red-teaming replaces the need for any other form of evaluation entirely
questions.explanation: Standard evaluation (perplexity, human ratings, comparison metrics) measures how well a system performs on typical inputs, whereas red-teaming specifically probes for how the system can be made to fail or misbehave — a complementary, not identical, activity.

questions.question: Why is it a mistake to treat red-teaming as a one-time, pre-launch-only activity?
options: Red-teaming is never useful at any point in a system's lifecycle
New failure modes continue to be discovered over time, including by real users after launch, so ongoing red-teaming remains valuable rather than a single pre-release checkbox
Red-teaming can only be performed once per model, ever, due to technical limitations
Standard evaluation metrics already cover everything red-teaming would find
questions.explanation: Failure modes aren't necessarily all discoverable before launch — new ones surface over time, including from real-world use — so treating red-teaming as an ongoing practice rather than a single pre-launch gate better matches how failure modes actually get discovered.

questions.question: Why is red-teaming that surfaces failure modes the original team didn't anticipate particularly valuable?
options: It isn't valuable; only anticipated failure modes matter
The most useful red-teaming often reveals blind spots — issues the team wouldn't have thought to test for on their own, which standard evaluation checklists would also miss
Unanticipated failure modes are always impossible to actually find
This kind of red-teaming only applies to non-generative systems
questions.explanation: Since teams naturally test for what they already expect, red-teaming's real value often comes from surfacing genuinely unanticipated failure modes — the kind that a checklist built from known risks would never catch.

questions.question: What do the standard evaluation metrics covered earlier in this course primarily tell you, according to this lesson?
options: How a system performs on typical, expected inputs
How the system behaves when someone deliberately tries to break it
Whether the system contains any harmful content whatsoever
The exact number of parameters in the underlying model
questions.explanation: The lesson explains that standard metrics like perplexity and human evaluation mostly reflect performance on typical, expected inputs, not deliberate adversarial probing.

questions.question: What does red-teaming specifically aim to do, per this lesson?
options: Deliberately try to elicit bad behavior from a generative system, like generating harmful content or leaking sensitive information
Measure how quickly a model can generate typical, well-formed responses
Replace the need for any other form of evaluation entirely
Only test image generation models, never text generation
questions.explanation: Red-teaming is defined in the lesson as deliberately probing a system to produce harmful content, leak information, or otherwise fail in ways standard evaluation wouldn't surface.

questions.question: Why does the lesson recommend ongoing red-teaming rather than a single pre-launch pass?
options: Because new failure modes get discovered continuously, including by real users after launch
Because red-teaming can only ever be performed exactly once per model
Because pre-launch testing always catches every possible failure mode
Because ongoing red-teaming has no additional benefit over a single pass
questions.explanation: The lesson warns against treating red-teaming as a one-time, pre-launch activity, since new failure modes continue to surface over time, including from real-world use after launch.

questions.question: Why is red-teaming that surfaces unanticipated failure modes considered especially valuable, according to this lesson?
options: Because the most valuable red-teaming often surfaces failure modes the original team didn't think to look for
Because only anticipated failure modes are worth testing for
Because unanticipated failure modes are always impossible to discover through testing
Because red-teaming can only test failure modes already covered by standard evaluation
questions.explanation: The lesson highlights that red-teaming's real value often comes from revealing blind spots — failure modes a checklist built from known risks would never have caught.

questions.question: How does this lesson connect red-teaming for generative systems to material covered later in the curriculum?
options: It connects directly to the security-mindset thinking that reappears in the eval-and-security track later in the curriculum
It has no connection to any other track in the curriculum
It replaces the need for the eval-and-security track entirely
It is only relevant to the computer vision track, not security
questions.explanation: The lesson explicitly ties this security-mindset approach to generative failure modes back to the eval-and-security track that appears later in the curriculum.
